citeAs: Amini, A., Gabriel, S., Lin, S., Koncel-Kedziorski, R., Choi, Y., and Hajishirzi, H. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319.
creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI)
description: MathQA is a large-scale dataset of 37,200 math word problems with corresponding multiple-choice options and aligned operation programs. It significantly enhances the AQuA dataset by providing fully-specified operational programs using a new operation-based representation language covering multiple math domain categories (Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, General, Other).
name: MathQA
publisher: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 validators reviewed each annotated program; at least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank the operation program as valid for it to be selected.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations are valid. Agreement between expert validation and crowd-sourcing validation was 87%. The alignment validation accuracy across categories was 94.64%. For problem categorization, human annotator agreement was 84% and their agreement with the model was 74.5%.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Figure Eight (https://www.figure-eight.com) — a custom dynamic annotation platform built on top of Figure Eight was used for crowd-sourced annotation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. The platform dynamically calculated intermediate results after each operation submission. Valid arguments were restricted to numbers in the problem, constants in the problem category, and previous calculations. Programs were only accepted if they included some numbers from the problem and whose final calculation was very close to the correct numeric solution. Annotators were randomly evaluated through pre-defined test questions and had to maintain an accuracy threshold to continue annotating; if accuracy dropped below the threshold, their previous annotations were labeled as untrusted and re-added to the annotation pool.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that the AQuA dataset contains significant noise including problems with incorrect solutions, problems unsolvable without brute-force enumeration, and rationales that contain few or none of the steps required to solve the problem. Many problems are near-duplicates with slight changes not reflected in rationales, leading to incorrect solutions. The paper also notes that the representation language omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely non-numeric. The paper mentions that the operation-based representation language can help reduce the influence of statistical bias in datasets like AQuA.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset (GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems) and annotating them with formal operation programs using crowdsourcing. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies, and then crowd workers used a dynamic annotation platform to align each problem with an operation program. Annotation expansion was also performed by finding closely similar problems (using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words) and extending annotations to cover more problems.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the AQuA (AQUA-RAT) dataset, which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems with rationales, expanded from a set of 30,000 seed problems through crowdsourcing.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely non-numeric. The representation language does not cover all math operations (e.g., factorization is not defined). Sequence problems requiring pattern understanding are currently unsolvable. The categorization strategy can be noisy. Model performance is still significantly lower than human performance, indicating the dataset poses challenges. Some problems in the original AQuA dataset are unsolvable or have multiple interpretations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion was performed: closely similar problems were found using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, numeric values were replaced with generic numbers, and annotations were expanded to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AQuA dataset was carefully studied and filtered. Problems were categorized into math domains using term frequencies (n-gram frequency). Unsolvable problems were identified and excluded, including: problems with no words, sequence problems, problems requiring options to solve, non-numeric problems, and near-duplicates. The dataset was split 80/12/8% into training/dev/test sets.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance interpretable AI for math problem solving, which could benefit educational applications and automated tutoring systems. The operation-based formalism improves model interpretability, making it easier to understand how models arrive at solutions.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluating neural models for math word problem solving; developing interpretable math problem solvers that map problems to operation programs; research on logical reasoning over natural language; semantic parsing of math word problems.
